Author: N.Tukaramji
Bench: N.Tukaramji
 The Honourable Sri Justice N.Tukaramji
 Criminal Petition No. 10423 Of 2024
Order:

This petition is filed under Section 528 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (for short 'the BNSS) seeking quashment of the proceedings in C.C.No.6598 of 2024, dated 02.05.2024 on the file of XV Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate at Nampally, Hyderabad.
2. Heard Mr.T.Yogesh, learned counsel for petitioner, Mr.Jithender Rao Veeramalla, learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing for the respondent No.1-State.

3. The petitioner is arrayed as accused No.4 in C.C No.6598 of 2024 facing accusation under Sections 498-A, 323, 506, 417 r/w. 34 of IPC and Sections 3, 4 and 6 of Dowry Prohibition Act,1961.
4.
The brief facts of the case are that Accused No. 1 and the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant were married according to Hindu rites and traditions.

At the time of the marriage, the parents of the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant allegedly provided dowry to Accused Nos. 1, 2, and 3,
consisting of Rs.20,00,000 in cash, 500 grams of gold ornaments, and 1 kilogram of silver ornaments.
Subsequently, Accused No. 1 and his parents allegedly subjected the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant to harassment with the intent of coercing her to bring additional dowry.
They are also alleged to have threatened her not to disclose the harassment to her parents, warning that failure to comply would result in her being killed.
On 26.11.2023, the mother-in-law of the defacto complainant allegedly initiated a dispute regarding the gold ornaments and demanded further dowry.
On 30.11.2023, the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant, accompanied by her parents, visited her matrimonial home in an attempt to amicably resolve the matter.
However, Accused No. 1 and his parents allegedly abused the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant and her parents in vulgar language, following which Accused No. 1 ordered her to leave the house.

On 03.12.2023, Accused No. 1 telephoned the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant, informing her of his sudden travel to the United States, purportedly to attend to his brother, Accused No. 4, who was hospitalized.

When the Respondent No.2/defacto complainant requested to accompany him,

sentences.text:
After reaching the United States,
Accused No. 1 is said to have gradually reduced communication with the defacto complainant.

On occasions when she attempted to contact him, Accused No. 4 allegedly answered the calls, spoke to her in a rude and abusive manner, warned her to 'stay within her limits,' threatened her with adverse consequences, and used vulgar language.
5. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that he did not even attended the marriage of his brother/Accused No.1, and Respondent No.2/defacto complainant.
He asserts that he has been residing in the United States since 2020 and that the immigration stamp on his passport, dated January 2020, remains unchallenged by the respondents.
Furthermore, even as per the allegations made by Respondent No.2/defacto complainant, the only act attributed to the petitioner is that he allegedly spoke to her in a rude manner.
Such an allegation, even if taken at its face value, does not constitute the offence of 'cruelty' as defined under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code.
Accordingly, the petitioner has prayed for the quashing of the criminal proceedings initiated against him.
6. The learned Additional Public Prosecutor contended that the complainant has specifically alleged an overt act on the part of the petitioner.
It was further submitted that the offence of 'cruelty' under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code encompasses not only physical cruelty but also mental cruelty.
The merits of the allegations, however, are matters to be adjudicated by the trial court at the appropriate stage.
Therefore, any interference at this preliminary stage would risk prejudicing and impeding the regular course of the judicial process.
7. I have considered the submissions of the learned counsels and perused the materials placed on record.

8. Upon a careful examination of the complaint and the statements recorded during the investigation, it appears that the role attributed to the petitioner is confined solely to allegations of having used rude and abusive language, accompanied by threats, during telephonic conversations.
9. The specific allegation against the petitioner is that, after Accused No. 1 arrived in the United States, he gradually reduced communication with the defacto-complainant.
Whenever she attempted to contact him to ascertain his whereabouts, it was occasionally Accused No.4/the petitioner, who answered the calls.

On such occasions, he allegedly spoke to her in a rude manner,
abused and admonished her to 'stay within her limits,' instructed her not to call his brother, and purportedly threatened her with adverse consequences while using vulgar language.
10. Beyond this solitary reference, no other specific, much less overt, act is attributed to the petitioner.
The uncontroverted assertion that the petitioner never resided with Respondent No. 2 also remains on record.
Furthermore, the statements of other witnesses examined by the police during the investigation do not disclose any independent allegation against the petitioner.
Consequently, the accusations against him appear vague, unsubstantiated, and lacking in material particulars.

sentences.text: It is well-settled law, as reaffirmed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand, (2010) 7 SCC 667, that while allegations under Section 498A IPC must be addressed with seriousness, courts must remain vigilant to prevent the mechanical implication of relatives without specific and credible allegations of their active participation in the alleged offence.

entities.text: Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand, (2010) 7 SCC 667
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Similarly,
in Geeta Mehrotra v. State of U.P., (2012) 10 SCC 741, it was held that bald and omnibus allegations,
unsupported by material particulars, cannot justify the prosecution of distant relatives.

entities.text: Geeta Mehrotra v. State of U.P., (2012) 10 SCC 741
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Most recently, in Kahkashan Kausar v. State of Bihar, (2022) 6 SCC 599, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the mere roping in of distant relatives or in-laws--without clear and credible assertions of active involvement in acts amounting to cruelty under Section 498A--constitutes an abuse of the process of law.

entities.text: Kahkashan Kausar v. State of Bihar, (2022) 6 SCC 599
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 12. In State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, the Supreme Court enumerated illustrative categories of cases where the inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC may be invoked to quash criminal proceedings.

entities.text: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, it also cautioned that where allegations, taken at face value, disclose the commission of an offence, proceedings should not be scuttled prematurely.
13. In the present case, the alleged verbal abuses and threats are supported solely by the uncorroborated testimony of the de facto complainant, without any independent evidence.

Even if these allegations are assumed to be true in their entirety, they fall short of disclosing a prima facie case of the petitioner's involvement so as to satisfy the essential ingredients of Section 498A IPC.
In such circumstances, the continuation of criminal proceedings against the petitioner would amount to an abuse of the process of law.
14. Accordingly, this Criminal Petition is allowed.

The proceedings against the petitioner/Accused No. 4 in C.C. No. 6598 of 2024, dated 02.05.2024, pending before the Court of the XV Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Nampally, Hyderabad, are hereby quashed.
